newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia dock strike paralyzes main Pacific port.
newsitem.headline: Colombia dock strike paralyzes main Pacific port.

text.p: Dock workers launched a strike at Colombia's main Pacific coast port on Wednesday, paralysing all operations including key coffee and sugar exports, port operators said.

The port of Buenaventura handles about 25,000 tons of cargo a day and is shipment point for about 60 percent of the country's coffee exports and all its sugar exports. Authorities estimated the privatised port would lose about $500,000 for every day of the strike.

Dockers approved a strike motion late on Tuesday and began picketing all entrances to the port on Wednesday. They are calling for higher wages, sickness and injury benefits and changes in the way they are currently contracted.
"All port activities are paralysed due to dockers blockading all port entrances," said Carlos Rojas, head of Buenaventura private customs agent Pan Servicios.
The National Federation of Coffee Growers, meanwhile, advised coffee exporters to avoid the port until the strike was resolved, one private trader said.

The federation declined to comment on the situation. As yet it is unclear whether shipments that normally pass through Buenaventura, primarily for Asian markets, will be delayed or sent via the Caribbean coast ports, which currently handle about 40 percent of Colombia's coffee exports.

The strike, headed by dockers' union SINTRAMARITIMOS, came after month-long talks between workers, port authorities and private contractors, known as primary or secondary operators, collapsed. Union leaders could not be reached for comment.

Dock work is Buenaventura's main source of employment. Work opportunities were slashed when the port was privatised in 1991. About 2,000 dockers now work at the port and earn an average of between $50 and $80 per month.
